rationale: A wins because its angles are cleaner reporter assignments, not just topic buckets. "Khan Academy is putting AI tutors in front of 1 million students. The study saying it works hasn't been peer-reviewed" gives an education data reporter a real tension, while B's "A nonprofit is giving an AI tutor to teachers for free while the rest of ed-tech charges per seat" blows past the supplied facts and turns a proof need into a headline. B has bones, but it keeps making the founder pay interest on claims the update did not deposit.
gaps_in_A: "districts are signing on to expand to 1 million students based on a study" overclaims causation; the update says the study and rollout arrive together, not that districts signed because of the study.
"While VC-backed EdTech companies charge districts" imports a market contrast not in the update; make it a proof question, not a premise.
"a body of research on productive failure and desirable difficulty argues" may be a useful reporting path, but it is outside the supplied facts and needs sourcing before it sits in the angle.
gaps_in_B: "while the rest of ed-tech charges per seat" is the worst move in the set: broad, unsupported, and sitting in the headline where it can do the most damage.
"one of the largest AI-tutoring deployments" is an invented ranking unless Khan can prove it against the market.
"landing in named districts" pretends the update supplied district names; it did not.
"education reporter or learning-science writer at a thoughtful education or policy outlet" is still soft. "Thoughtful" is a compliment, not a beat.
